German police said they had detained a suspect after fire broke out at a historic mountain guest house known as the “Eagle’s Nest,” used as a retreat by Nazi officials, including the dictator Adolf Hitler.
Around 200 firefighters and emergency personnel in the area around Berchtesgaden in the southern region of Bavaria were battling the flames after the building, known as the Kehlsteinhaus, caught fire on Friday, police said.
Police are investigating whether the suspect, who was detained close to the scene, was connected to the fire, they said in a statement.

Tokyo —
In the 18 days Runa spent in a police cell in Japan, she wrote about how much she yearned to come home.
The teenager missed her mother’s cooking, her hugs, and their small, ordinary rituals of life together – reading, shopping, and singing.
“Please, I beg you. I want to see my mom,” she scribbled in a notepad given to her during her detention, seen by CNN.
Runa’s incarceration – and death months after her release – is now the subject of a lawsuit brought by her mother against Hyogo Prefectural Police alleging unlawful arrest and detention. Proceedings opened this week in a case that’s shone a spotlight on Japan’s treatment of juvenile suspects.

When Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva walked out of the Federal Police headquarters in Curitiba, Brazil, on November 8, 2019, hundreds of supporters were waiting for him.
Many had been there, on and off, for much of the 580 days he spent behind bars, keeping vigil outside the building and calling out “good morning,” “good afternoon” and “good night” as they defended his innocence and demanded his freedom.
Lula emerged into the crowd and did what he had done best throughout his political life: he gave a speech. “They didn’t imprison a man,” he declared. “They tried to kill an idea. But you can’t kill an idea.”
Seven years later, Lula is Brazil’s president and is again fighting to prove that the ideas of his movement can break through the country’s deep polarization, a wave of new corrupti...
